title: Formal Malay: letters, essays and the news
goal: Writing and reading formal Malay — the opposite end from unit 12, and the layer that decides whether your writing is acceptable in Malaysian schools, offices and government business.
bekal: writing a formal Malay letter with the standard layout and phrases
reading Malaysian news without stumbling over administrative terms
knowing six Indonesian habits to drop from your written Malay

notes: **Karangan** = essay, composition. It's the standard Malaysian term for school writing, and it's graded in the SPM exam. Types: *karangan berformat* (formatted: letters, reports, speeches) and *karangan tidak berformat* (free: essays, stories).
**Elak / mengelak** = to avoid. *Kena elak* = must be avoided.
**Teguran** = a correction, a gentle reprimand. *Terima kasih atas teguran* is a polite, fitting thing to say when someone corrects your mistake.
**Sepatutnya** = should, ought to. *Patut* and its family (*patutnya*, *sepatutnya*, *patutlah* = no wonder) are very productive in Malaysia.
**Banyakkan** = do more of, increase. Note the *-kan* again — the Malay habit covered in unit 10; it comes up constantly in advice and instructions.

grammars.title: Six Indonesian habits that give your writing away
body: Many Malay learning materials online are actually Indonesian. These habits tell a Malaysian reader straight away that the writer learned from Indonesian sources. None of them is a grammar mistake — they're all word choice and spelling.

head: Indonesian habit
What Malaysia uses
rows: *bagaimana* is correct, but written Malay prefers *bagaimanakah*, *sahaja*
*di mana* as a linking word ("rapat di mana kami…", like English "where")
⚠️ Wrong in both standards; Malay uses *tempat* or *yang*

after: Rows three and four matter most: **Malay keeps long forms that Indonesian has shortened.** *Sahaja* (not *saja*), *kerana* (not *karena*), *bahagian* (not *bagian*), *baharu* (not *baru*, though *baru* is also accepted). In speech the short forms are used; in formal writing, the long ones.
⚠️ **An *h* that Indonesian has dropped is often still there in Malay**: *faham*, *sihat*, *khabar*, *bahagian*, *sahaja*, *tahniah*, *mahu*. It's a pattern you can rely on as a first guess.

grammars.title: The layout of a formal letter
body: Malaysian formal letters follow a standard layout taught in schools and used throughout government. The structure is like a formal English letter, but the phrases are fixed formulas.

head: Part
Malay
English equivalent
rows: **Dengan segala hormatnya, perkara di atas adalah dirujuk.**
With respect, I refer to the above matter.
*3. Sehubungan itu, saya memohon jasa baik tuan…*
I would therefore be grateful if you could…

after: Two things are truly Malaysian. First, **numbered paragraphs**: the body of a formal Malaysian letter is almost always split into numbered paragraphs (2., 3., 4.), with the first paragraph unnumbered. Second, the **motto** — government letters carry a motto in quotation marks above the signature, such as *"BERKHIDMAT UNTUK NEGARA"* (Serving the Nation) or *"MALAYSIA MADANI"*.
**Perkara** = subject, matter (of a letter). It's written in capitals and underlined — this is compulsory and people notice.

blocks.text: Malaysian news uses a layer of administrative vocabulary that never comes up in conversation. These are the words that most often stop readers in their tracks:

The five most important: **kerajaan** (government), **pilihan raya** (election), **mahkamah** (court), **belanjawan** (budget) and **mangsa** (victim). They're on the front page almost every day, and one of them — *kerajaan* — can make a whole story read wrong if you take it to mean a monarchy (from *raja*, king).
⚠️ **Mangsa** means **victim**. *Mangsa banjir* = flood victims, *mangsa kemalangan* = accident victims. (In Indonesian *mangsa* means prey — a trap if you've learned from Indonesian sources.)

blocks.title: How to read the paper without giving up
items: **Start with stories you already know about** — football, weather, entertainment. You can guess from context.
**Read all the headlines first, then pick one.** Malay headlines are very dense and full of abbreviations.
**Don't look up every word.** Read a whole paragraph first, then check the two or three words that block you most.
**Kamus Dewan online** is the standard reference — free and published by Dewan Bahasa dan Pustaka.
**Berita Harian**, **Utusan Malaysia**, **Harian Metro**, **Astro Awani**, **Berita RTM** — all available online.

blocks.text: The module closes with one paragraph written in the three registers you've learned. If you can read all three and know where each one belongs, this module has done its job.
*Weh, aku tak dapat datang esok la. Ada hal sikit kat rumah. Korang pergi dulu, nanti aku jumpa kat sana kot. Sorry ya.*
Everyday polite register (most of this module)
*Maaf, saya tak dapat datang esok. Ada hal sikit kat rumah. Awak orang pergi dulu, nanti saya cuba jumpa kat sana. Maaf sangat.*

*Dengan segala hormatnya, saya memohon maaf kerana tidak dapat hadir pada esok hari disebabkan urusan keluarga yang tidak dapat dielakkan. Sehubungan itu, saya memohon jasa baik tuan untuk meneruskan program tersebut tanpa kehadiran saya. Sekian, terima kasih.*

Notice that it's not just word choice that changes: the formal register uses **long sentences with full affixes** (*disebabkan*, *dielakkan*, *kehadiran*), while the street register drops almost all affixes. Malay stretches further along this scale than English does, and mastering both ends is the mark of a mature speaker.

blocks.title: What now?
items: You've made it through twenty units. What's left isn't knowledge, but practice hours.
**Read one Malaysian news story a day.** Ten minutes, no more.
**Watch one news bulletin a week** without subtitles.
**Find one Malaysian to talk to.** This makes the biggest difference.
**Go back to unit 3 and the false-friends list** whenever you're unsure. It's the page people reopen most.
*Selamat maju jaya — dan jumpa lagi di Kuala Lumpur.* (All the best — see you in Kuala Lumpur.)
